title: Items banned on a plane: The complete 2026 list | Grey
summary: Items banned on a plane range from lithium batteries to certain liquids and sharp objects. See the full 2026 list by category. Compare before you pack.
body_markdown:
Some everyday items you wouldn't think twice about packing can become a problem at airport security. That perfume you use every day, the power bank you carry everywhere, your favourite pocket knife or even a bottle of water could cause problems at airport security if you don't know the rules. What seems harmless in your handbag or suitcase may be restricted or completely prohibited on an aircraft.


Items banned on a plane generally fall into six groups: explosives and flammables, compressed gases, corrosives, toxic substances, lithium batteries above permitted limits, and sharp or blunt weapons. Some items are prohibited in carry-on luggage but allowed in checked baggage, while others cannot be carried on an aircraft at all. Restrictions vary depending on your airline, destination and aviation authority.


This is why checking your luggage before heading to the airport matters. You don't want to arrive at security only to have an expensive item confiscated, face unnecessary delays or risk missing your flight.


In this article, we'll cover more than 200 restricted and prohibited items, explain where they belong and help you understand what you can safely pack before your next trip.


## What items are banned on a plane entirely?


Six main hazard categories are prohibited from aircraft entirely: explosives, flammable materials, toxic substances, corrosives, radioactive materials and disabling devices. These items pose risks to passengers, crew and aircraft safety, so they cannot be packed in either carry-on or checked luggage.


## What is banned from hand luggage but allowed in the hold?


Some items are too sharp, heavy or potentially dangerous to be carried inside the aircraft cabin but can travel safely in checked baggage. These include certain sharp objects, work tools, sporting equipment and liquids that exceed airport security limits. If you're unsure whether something belongs in your hand luggage, check the rules before packing to avoid having it confiscated at security.


Category Items not allowed in hand luggage


Sharp objects Pocket knives, box cutters, loose razor blades, large scissors and other sharp-bladed items. Small scissors may be permitted depending on blade length and local security rules.


Tools
Hammers, screwdrivers, wrenches, pliers, drills, saws and other heavy tools that could cause injury or be used as weapons.


Sporting goods Baseball bats, cricket bats, golf clubs, hockey sticks, ski poles and pool cues. These are generally accepted in checked baggage, subject to airline size and weight restrictions.


Liquids above the cabin limit Shampoo, perfume, lotions, creams, gels and beverages in containers exceeding 100 ml (3.4 oz). These generally belong in checked baggage rather than your cabin bag.


‍


## What is banned from the hold but allowed in the cabin?


Certain battery-powered devices and spare lithium batteries must travel in the cabin rather than checked baggage because of the fire risk they pose. According to the FAA's[PackSafe guidance](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe) , power banks and spare batteries must remain with passengers, subject to capacity limits.


Item Cabin baggage rules Watt-hour (Wh) limits


Lithium battery-powered devices Devices such as laptops, phones and cameras can generally travel in the cabin. Up to 100 Wh generally allowed. Between 100 and 160 Wh requires airline approval. Above 160 Wh is prohibited on passenger aircraft.


Power banks Must be carried in hand luggage, not checked baggage. Terminals should be protected against short circuits. Up to 100 Wh generally allowed; 100–160 Wh requires airline approval. Above 160 Wh is prohibited.


E-cigarettes and vapes
Must remain in cabin baggage. Charging or use onboard is prohibited. Battery capacity restrictions and airline rules apply.


Spare lithium cells Loose rechargeable and non-rechargeable lithium batteries must travel in the cabin with protected terminals. Up to 100 Wh generally allowed; 100–160 Wh requires airline approval


‍


## Country and airline differences you should check


Packing your suitcase according to your airline's baggage policy is a good start, but it doesn't mean every item will automatically be allowed throughout your journey. Air travel restrictions operate at different levels: national aviation regulations, airport security requirements, transit-country rules and individual airline policies. An item permitted on your departure flight could still cause problems when you land or pass through another airport.


Here are three important differences to consider before travelling.


### 1. Smart luggage restrictions


Airlines have specific rules for suitcases containing built-in lithium batteries. If the battery is removable, you may be allowed to check in the suitcase after removing it and carrying the battery in the cabin. However, smart luggage with non-removable batteries exceeding permitted limits may be refused altogether. Always check your airline's battery policy before purchasing or packing one. While preparing for your trip, a[Grey travel eSIM](https://grey.co/lifestyle) can also help you stay connected when you land, without having to search for a local SIM card at the airport.


### 2. Transit airport security


Connecting flights can introduce additional restrictions because you may have to pass through security screening again. For example, liquids purchased at an airport duty-free shop may be confiscated during transit if they are not properly sealed in an approved tamper-evident bag with proof of purchase. Check the transit airport's requirements before buying perfumes, alcohol or other liquids.


### 3. Local customs and import restrictions


Some countries prohibit items that airlines might otherwise allow onboard. Australia, for example, has strict biosecurity requirements covering fresh food, plants and animal products. Thailand also prohibits the importation of e-cigarettes and vaping products. Travellers should check destination-country customs rules rather than assuming cabin or checked baggage approval means an item can enter the country. ## **What happens if a banned item is found?**


Finding a prohibited item in your luggage doesn't always mean you'll be denied boarding or face legal trouble. What happens next depends on the item, where it is discovered and whether it poses a safety risk. Airport security officers and airline staff follow specific procedures to deal with prohibited items, ranging from confiscation to reporting dangerous goods to the relevant authorities.


Here are three possible outcomes:


### **1. Confiscation and disposal**


If security finds an item that is prohibited in hand luggage but permitted in checked baggage, you may be given the opportunity to return to the check-in counter and repack it, provided time and airport procedures allow. Otherwise, the item may be surrendered or confiscated. Oversized liquids, pocket knives and prohibited tools are common examples. Some airports also provide facilities for mailing certain items home, although this isn't guaranteed.


### **2. Fines and legal penalties**


Carrying dangerous goods, undeclared explosives, or prohibited weapons can have more serious consequences. Depending on the country's laws and the circumstances, you could face financial penalties, questioning by airport police, prosecution or refusal of carriage. In the United States, for example, the FAA can impose substantial civil penalties for dangerous goods violations. The severity depends on the nature of the violation and applicable regulations.


### **3. Dangerous goods reporting**


When airport staff discover hazardous materials, they may isolate the affected baggage, prevent it from being loaded and notify the airline's dangerous goods personnel. Suspected serious incidents can also be reported to airport authorities and national aviation regulators. These reports help investigators identify safety risks and prevent similar incidents on future flights.


## Frequently asked questions about items banned on a plane


### **1. Can you take a power bank on a plane?**


Yes, you can bring a power bank on a plane, but it must travel in your hand luggage rather than checked baggage. Most airlines allow power banks up to 100 watt-hours (Wh) without special approval. Those between 100 and 160 Wh generally require airline approval, while anything above 160 Wh is prohibited on passenger aircraft. Always protect the terminals against short circuits.


### **2. Are nail scissors allowed in hand luggage?**


Yes, small nail scissors are generally permitted in hand luggage, provided they meet the airport's blade-length restrictions. Rules vary by country: some authorities use a 6 cm limit, while US rules generally allow scissors with blades shorter than 4 inches. Larger scissors may need to go in checked baggage.


### **3. Can you fly with aerosols?**


Yes, personal-care aerosols such as deodorant and hairspray are generally allowed, subject to airline and aviation authority restrictions. In hand luggage, they must normally be in containers of 100 ml or less. Checked baggage may allow larger toiletry aerosols, commonly up to 500 ml per item, subject to quantity and packaging limits.


### **4. What liquids are banned on a plane?**


Flammable fuels, certain chemicals, corrosive liquids and other dangerous substances are prohibited from passenger aircraft. Ordinary liquids such as shampoo, perfume and drinks are generally allowed in checked baggage. However, hand luggage usually has a 100 ml container limit under standard airport security rules, although some airports operate approved alternative screening systems.


### **5. Can you bring food through airport security?**


Yes, most solid foods, including sandwiches, biscuits, bread, fruit and packaged snacks, can pass through airport security. However, foods with liquid, gel or spreadable consistency, such as yoghurt, jam, sauces and peanut butter, generally fall under cabin liquid restrictions. International travellers should also check destination customs rules because some countries restrict fresh produce, meat and dairy products.


### 6. What happens if security finds a banned item?


The outcome depends on the item and the applicable aviation rules. Harmless restricted items, such as oversized liquids or prohibited cabin tools, may be confiscated or returned to you for repacking in checked baggage if permitted. Dangerous goods, explosives and prohibited weapons can result in seizure, questioning, financial penalties or prosecution. Serious incidents may also be reported to aviation authorities.
